speaker: Doctor
text: The rash appearing after the fever subsides is a classic sign of roseola, but I need to rule out other causes. Did you notice any swelling in your lymph nodes, particularly around your neck or ears, while you had the fever?

speaker: Patient
text: No, I did not notice any swelling in her neck or ears while she had the fever. She seemed otherwise normal aside from the high temperature and the seizure.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is the patient experiencing any cough, runny nose, or other respiratory symptoms? Also, has she had any recent contact with people who are sick?

speaker: Patient
text: She has no cough or runny nose, and her breathing is completely normal. We haven't had any contact with other sick people recently.

speaker: Doctor
text: Does the rash blanch, or turn white, when you press on it with a clear glass? Also, is she back to her normal energy levels and appetite now that the fever is gone?

speaker: Patient
text: Yes, the rash turns white when I press on it with a glass. She is back to her normal self, eating well and playing happily now that the fever has resolved.

speaker: Doctor
text: The blanching rash and her return to normal health strongly suggest a benign viral exanthem. Do you recall the exact temperature of the fever, and was the seizure generalized, involving shaking of the entire body?

speaker: Patient
text: Yes, the fever reached 40.5°C (104.9°F). The seizure was generalized, involving shaking of her entire body for about a minute.

speaker: Doctor
text: This presentation of high fever followed by a rash and a febrile seizure is highly characteristic of Roseola Infantum. Was the rash most prominent on her trunk, and did it spread to her face or limbs?

speaker: Patient
text: Yes, the rash started on her trunk and then spread to her arms and legs. It hasn't really spread to her face, though.

speaker: Doctor
text: This clinical picture is classic for Roseola Infantum, also known as Exanthem Subitum. DIAGNOSIS READY: Roseola Infantum
